Lakota

Lakota is a people with distinct bands, communities, and governments across the northern Plains and into Canada. This guide introduces that wider history and links to separately sourced community pages.

01

Identity and homelands

Lakota includes distinct oyate and governments; Sicangu Lakota at Rosebud is one particular community within that wider people.

Read the sources [1] Rosebud Sioux Tribe

02

Historical context

Rosebud’s history traces westward movements, buffalo hunting, treaty violations, and the leadership of Sinte Gleska, Spotted Tail.

Read the sources [1] Rosebud Sioux Tribe

03

Living communities and further study

The Rosebud government’s public information connects history with contemporary governance and cultural preservation. Other Lakota nations need their own profiles and sources.

Read the sources [2] Rosebud Sioux Tribe

04

Lakota and the Seven Council Fires

The Aktá Lakota Museum places the Tetonwan within the wider Očeti Šakówiŋ, often called the Seven Council Fires. The museum lists seven Tetonwan bands. In its spellings they are Hunkpapa, Sicangu, Itazipo, Sihasapa, Oglala, Oohenumpa, and Minniconjou. Individual community accounts use their own spellings and describe the governments and places with which they are connected.

Read the sources [3] Aktá Lakota Museum & Cultural Center

05

Communities across the Plains

The community pages below show several kinds of Lakota connection. Oglala's public account connects Pine Ridge with South Dakota and Nebraska. Standing Rock describes Dakota and Lakota communities in North Dakota and South Dakota. Fort Peck's own introduction describes distinct Assiniboine and Sioux peoples in Montana, including Hunkpapa in its Sioux history. The museum's account also connects Hunkpapa history with Wood Mountain in Canada.

Read the sources [7] Oglala Sioux Tribe [4] Standing Rock Sioux Tribe [5] Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes of the Fort Peck Indian Reservation [3] Aktá Lakota Museum & Cultural Center

06

The Black Hills and the plains

The Smithsonian's homelands lesson presents the Black Hills in South Dakota through attributed Lakota accounts of place and origin. It also describes the role of bison in northern Plains food, clothing, tools, and community life. The authors and institutions named on the page provide a starting point for following those accounts in context.

Read the sources [8] Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian · Native Knowledge 360°

07

Reading the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty

The National Archives presents the treaty text and identifies the parties using the names recorded in the treaty. Article II sets out land provisions, including the historical reservation described in the Archives introduction. Article VII describes compulsory school attendance under conditions stated in the treaty. These clauses help readers place later community histories of land and schooling in context.

Read the sources [9] National Archives

08

Language and learning

Indiana University's language portal introduces Lakota as part of the Siouan language family and points readers to course materials and recordings. Oglala Lakota College and Sinte Gleska University describe their own teaching programs. These provide separate ways to learn about Lakota language, history, and community education.

Read the sources [10] Indiana University · Center for Language Technology [11] Oglala Lakota College [12] Sinte Gleska University
